newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Angola's UNITA slammed for landmines, attacks.
newsitem.headline: Angola's UNITA slammed for landmines, attacks.

text.p: An Angolan peace commission, including the United Nations, condemned the former rebel UNITA movement on Friday for laying landmines and mounting attacks in northern areas of the country.
The joint peace commission, which includes representatives of the government and UNITA, is overseeing the implementation of a 1994 peace treaty to end Angola's 20-year civil war.

But the joint commission criticised UNITA for attacking the towns of Muaquesse and Caxinagagi in the northeastern diamond province of Lunda Norte, a statement from the U.N. Observer Mission in Angola (MONUA) said.
The towns were retaken by the government army in June during skirmishes over control of the diamond area in the northeast, mostly controlled by UNITA.
But last week the government, which is trying to extend control over the entire countryside, said UNITA had again seized the two towns.
The joint commission said UNITA had also planted landmines in two areas under its control in the northernmost Malange province.
"The joint commission condemns the two acts of remining that have been recently discovered in areas under UNITA's control in Malange," the U.N. statement said.

Angola is one of the world's most heavily mined countries. Britain's Princess Diana visited the country in January to push for a ban on landmines. Millions of dollars have been spent in landmine clearing operations in the country.
The joint commission also criticised the movement for "the obstacles that UNITA members have placed in the way of MONUA investigating teams".
The U.N. is tasked with verifying government and UNITA claims of contraventions of the peace accord.

It also urged both sides on Friday to avoid broadcasting unverified allegations and appealed to UNITA to end difficulties blocking demobilisation of former rebel soldiers at four demobilisation camps.

Under the peace pact UNITA troops have been disarmed since 1996 at 15 U.N.-supervised assembly camps around the country. Many of the camps have been closed as the soldiers are demobilised or integrated into a single national army.
